This is a good example of confusing the sum of parts for a whole. The original Eleanor Rigby is one of the Beatles’ masterpieces. It is economical in runtime and minimal in production, yet it is dripping with mystery, packing a huge punch with little and in little time. This overly-long and over-produced imitation replaces any mystery with boring bombast. A good cover is a metamorphosis of one creature into another of equal or greater beauty. Like the Star Wars sequels, this is a puppeteered corpse dressed in new clothes, relying on brash restatements of the original’s accoutrements while losing the soul to which those elements were subordinated and given purpose.

The growing percussion is brimming with dread, evoking the terror of the coal train. The lyrics drip out of the music. The extended/freeform brass section leads into palpably emotional singing, more crying out than anything else. The thundering finale is...how do you even describe it? Fury? Grief? Remembrance? Perhaps all three. As I said in another comment, I love songs that tell a story. Here, the song itself IS the story, or rather it's the whole performance rather than the lyrics alone. That might not make full sense, but it's hard to put into words what I think this accomplishes on emotional and sensual levels. I would've been entertained by a random African song but not mesmerized as I have been here. This pick was a masterstroke, edged out only by a deeper cut. Silver!! 🥈

I really thought I was going to be the only Japanese submission this round, but Nature finds a way. I think this is Claire? Such acumen befits her, and indeed, I do like me some City Pop. Thanks to her, we got a family tree of Japanese pop in this playlist (both entries are downstream from the Kayōkyoku genre & Haruomi Hosono in particular, I think). As they did with baseball, the Japanese took readily to American jazz & funk, creating this cool sound that dominated their musicscape, especially in the early 80s. This is probably going to be one of the more unjust and hypocritical no votes, especially from others' perspective. I like this song and am impressed by how on the same wavelength you were as me, but in the big world of Jpop, I like the more Yellow Magic Orchestra evolutionary strand of my song much more (this is definitely Eddie’s strand tho), & other strong entries won out. Forgive the electoral slight here and know that you still nailed it in the main, senpai.

The lyrics are fantastic ("you're moving on the back roads by the rivers of my memory" - that is really great stuff). This country pop sound just seizes me on a pre-rational level, but the beat is also just so enchanting. Something you happened upon here, intentionally or unintentionally, is that I LOVE songs with a quick, driving beat (e.g. Mick Fleetwood pounding that bass drum is what makes so many Fleetwood Mac songs work for me). The bass guitar and accompanying picking here are too much too deny. It may be a stereotype, but dang if it didn't claw its way tooth and nail up the pack and onto the podium. Bronze!! 🥉

I discovered this band via a collaboration w/ CHVRCHES, and they've become one of my favorites (they're not really known outside Japan). I thought of doing a Yellow Magic Orchestra song, as the electronica that they pioneered in late 70s Japan is and begat some of the best music ever made. This is the granddaughter of that sound, layering more recent JPop on a techno foundation. As much as I agree with Eddie about production/sound not being everything, sometimes production/sound is the whole point, as it is here (song is about a hardware store & its Aladdin-themed cleaning products lol). Claire got the Japan factor, but Nippon EDM is really my favorite in that musicscape. I used to listen to this type of stuff more in high school and college, and in digging into the depths of my interests for this round, I remembered how much I love this genre and am excited to return to it. If you liked this, I recommend their songs Onyankopon, Melos, and Zeami (most of you probably hate it tho lol).

I've said several times that for these "Songs X would love" rounds, you should really look for intersection of interests rather than a random pick, and the former clearly led you in the right direction here (I hate a ton of country music, so that's a dangerous guessing game).
